title: What comes out (Mark 7:14–23)
hookLine: it's not what goes in that defiles, but what comes out of the heart
last: TRADITION — KEEP THE HEART OF IT.

cards: A whole day of careful eating: vegetables, water, vitamins. Then someone cuts in on the highway, or a coworker takes credit for the work, and what comes out is something nobody's grandmother should hear.
Everything that went in was careful. What came out wasn't. After the argument about washed hands, Jesus calls the whole crowd back to him and says, listen, all of you, and understand.
Then he says something so short it sounds like a riddle.

teach.b: Here's the riddle, in the old King James Bible: "There is nothing from without a man, that entering into him can defile him: but the things which come out of him, those are they that defile the man."

Defile, in Greek, means to make common, to make ordinary something that was meant to be set apart. Later, indoors, the disciples ask him about it, and he's a bit exasperated again: "Are ye so without understanding also?"
Food goes into the stomach, he says, not into the heart, and then out again.
But "from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts," and he names a long list: thefts, murders, greed, deceit, envy, pride, foolishness. That's what really makes a person unclean.
Mark adds a short note of his own here; the King James words it purging all meats, and some Christian readers take it as Jesus declaring all foods clean.
Some Christians point to it when asked why they don't keep the food laws of the Torah.

Jews who keep kosher understand those laws as God's commandments to Israel, and keep them with devotion; and scholars differ on how much Mark's note meant at the time. Either way, the center of the teaching is the heart.
In the Bible, the heart isn't only feelings.
It's where you think, decide and choose: the kitchen where words get cooked before they're served. So Jesus moves the question from the plate to the source. Not only, what did I take in today?

how: Christians do not, as a rule, keep the Torah's food laws, and some point to this passage when asked why; some also practice an examination of conscience at the end of the day, looking back over what they said and did.

o: to spoil food by touching it with dirty hands
to break a rule by eating without washing
to make common what was meant to be set apart

games.q: you're asked what really makes a person unclean. what does Jesus say?
o: what comes out of the heart.
games.why: the things which come out of him, those are they that defile the man: from within, out of the heart.

practice: Replay the last day: not what you ate or watched, but what you said, the kind words, the sharp ones, the joke at someone's expense, the complaint you repeated.

Without punishing yourself, notice where each one came from: tired, scared, jealous, generous, glad. If you pray, you can ask God for a clean heart; if not, just choose one word you'd like to say more of.

wordCard.voice: Defile, what Jesus said doesn't come from the plate but from the heart: evil thoughts, not food, are what truly defile a person.

orig.note: Greek: to make common, to defile, from koinos, common, shared.

carryVoice: Your line: from the heart. What comes out shows what's inside. Day one hundred eighty-seven, complete.
